paragraphs.text: Men lived in Aoaz long before Aen. The men of those early days were stronger in magic and longer-lived than their descendants, and they raised great realms. Yet none of those realms had one crown over all men. That was Aen’s work: when he ended the War of Men he made the first united kingdom of men, and with his victory the First Age began.
paragraphs.note: That great realms of men stood before Aen and none had one crown over all men is the owner’s adoption of 25 October 2026 (K64).

sources.section: First Age ethnic and political history

paragraphs.text: The scholars of Parim and Selen give no years to those realms. They say only that they stood long before Aen, and they know them less from writing than from what they left behind: fields under the sea, a city broken across a narrow sea, halls beneath forts, doors sealed against the sea, a square of reefs and timbers that the ice gives back.

Not all of them were realms of men, and not all of them fell before Aen. The dwarves of every great range were once one realm beneath the seas, and the chart-islanders of the western arcs once kept a league of the sea; both lasted into the First Age. The mountain kings of the Kalioth upland ruled in the East through that same age and fell at its end.

The peoples of Aoaz are old, but its realms are young under their old names. The heirs of the fallen realms keep their names, and each heir keeps only a part of what was lost: a tongue, a law, a count, a door, a chart, a fire. They do not readily share what they keep, and most strangers know the old realms only by their traces.
No chronicle tells how Aen was born, what the old name of the First Men means, or where the dwarves first came from, and none of the fallen realms answers those questions.

plate.subject: a grey shallow sea at the lowest tide, with the tops of old field-walls and a low mound breaking the water

paragraphs.text: West of Aenor Isle the sea lies shallow over wide banks, and the fishers’ nets bring up field-walls, quern-stones and stones cut with twisted cords. At the lowest spring tides a reef breaks the water there like the top of a mound. The common speech calls the drowned land the Low Country, and the isle folk say the sea took it in one night, the Night of the Sea, long before Aen.

Its heirs keep its law without its name. In the grey downs and the red-oak forest the Orran tongue is still spoken, descent runs through mothers, and law is kept on cords. The Isle Houses of Aenor Isle are ruled by their eldest women, choose their queen in a tide-chamber at the turn of the tide, and give their dead to the tide; they keep that law without knowing why.

When the sea came, the Orran kingdoms of the river valleys rose from what was left, and their wars over a shrinking land ran on into the War of Men. The Orran houses that would not kneel to Aen took their cords into the grey downs and the red-oak forest. Under the Aenoran names of the Vale’s rivers and towns lie older Orran ones.

The giants of Hirolon keep the Eldest Cairn, to which a keeper adds one stone in every year since the sea came. Their cairn-keepers will say of the drowned land only that it was asked for too much. The Veiled of the downs say the same, and count the souring of their downs by the Black Roots as the second land to die of asking. The scholars of Parim do not agree whether the land was lost to its own nature or to what was asked of it.

Its own people called it Muzerar, and the cord-mothers named the city of their moot Ozelkak, the Many Halls. Its folk were Orran-speaking men of six beast-clans: Wolf, Bear, Eagle, Horse, Raven and Water. The Moot of Mothers at Ozelkak, a seat for the eldest cord-mother of every clan, ruled more land than Aenor ever held with no king and no crown. The hill giants raised its sea-dikes as partners, and the low fields gave three harvests a year.

The mothers drew on the magic of the place for the third harvest and for their long rule, and over the centuries the ground sank below the sea behind ever higher dikes. The giants warned the Moot, the mothers divided, and those who would draw harder won. Then a storm-tide broke the last dikes, and the sea took Ozelkak and the low fields in one night. In 4A 1748 the Eldest Cairn holds 7,436 stones.

plate.subject: fallen stone pillars in long coastal grass facing a narrow sea channel

paragraphs.text: Long before Aen the east coast of the Magical Lands and the East Lands were one land, joined by a broad neck where the Rift Sea now runs. One Eastern people held both shores, and the first great road of Aoaz ran over the neck. The common speech calls their realm the Bridge Kingdom.

The neck broke, and the sea came in from north and south until the two shores stood apart across a long rift. A city that stood on the neck broke in two. Its western half lies under the fungal belt of the Mushroom Forest beside Luv-zhise, whose ferries cross the drowned road. Its eastern half lies under the grass of the Delbiz coast, where the horse-fair is held among fallen pillars.

Its one tongue parted into the Eastern tongues. The valley people of Alerhia raised their first stair above the flood-line “so that the river and the gods would each have a place”, and the River Temples faith holds the river to be the oldest god anyone can see. The old roads end at Lenkei, where the elves of Eldafaen keep a treaty of passage longer than any crown has stood.

Before the neck broke the horse came west over it, and the riders of the Middle Lands and the horse-lords of Delbiz share the memory. The cedar came west too, and so did the ogres, which is why one people lives on both sides of a sea without being sailors. The ditches under Noleksun’s fields still drink from the canals of the old western march.

No chronicle tells what broke the land. The temple chronicles of Alerhia say that the gods divided it to end a war between two brothers. The oldest rolls of the rift-coast elves say that the western heir’s sorcerers woke something that sleeps beneath the East. The salt-boilers say it still breathes under the Hot Lake, and they count the year 4A 1655, when the Hot Lake breathed out over Mora, as its latest sign.

Its own name was Tarkia, from the Alerhic word for a bridge; the desert tellers call it Tarqis and the Stabilic ledgers Pontoseno, the old bridge. The city on the neck was Qadurum. Tarkia was a realm of stair-temples above the flood-line, of scribes who wrote the reed letters from which the Alerhic script descends, and of kings anointed at the river who bore the title Sara rabu, great king.

At its height Tarkia held more land than Aenor ever did: the western East Lands, the neck with Qadurum astride it, and the road west through the Zilin Hills and over the South Pass into the downs of Herez and Noleksun. A great king left two heirs, the realm split along its road, and in their war the neck broke. The western house faded among the hills of the Middle Lands, and the eastern half broke into river crowns.

plate.subject: seven stone forts along a dry upland ridge above dark mine-mouths

paragraphs.text: Erco’s seven forts stand on an old fortress line on the Kalioth, the dry upland of the southern East, and beneath them lie the halls of the mountain kings who once ruled there. The chroniclers of every other realm call their empire the Kalioth Crown, after the upland where its kings sat.

The Kalioth kings were Alerhic-speaking lords of mines and iron, who ruled mine-folk, desert tribes and the pass-houses of the Hardtmuth. Theirs was a fortress empire of heavy horse, iron, slave-worked mines and walled upland cities, and in the First Age it was the greatest power of the East. It never held Alerhia’s river crown, which defied it.

Its kings took Volgan’s side and paid him the Black Tribute of ships, grain and men, which Alerhia refused in 1A 1214. As Volgan’s ally the Crown held Herez, Noleksun and the South Pass for about a century, the only eastern realm that ever ruled land in the Middle Lands after the neck broke. At Dardan its host stood with Volgan’s and died there.

Afterwards its western garrisons starved. In 2A 12 the mine-lords of the southern mountains shut the passes against the beaten host and besieged the last king in his hall, and Erco was founded on the ruin. They walled up the last king’s iron diadem and would neither wear it nor melt it. The miners of Erco say that no miner may strike that wall.

In Herez and Noleksun the folk keep a word for eastern raiders and the stone forts the occupiers built on the downs. Miaed’s pass-houses remember the water and guides they sold to Volgan’s eastern clients. The provinces beyond the Melty Pass fell silent when the Crown fell, and it is not known what became of them.

The kings’ own court name for their empire was Rhabtarkia, the Greater Bridge Kingdom. They called themselves the restorers of the kingdom of the bridge and swore to rejoin the shores. They rose about 1A 500 and proclaimed Rhabtarkia about 1A 1000, and their height lay between 1A 900 and 1500, while Aenor declined under its bad kings.

Their seat on the Kalioth was Barzoth, the iron height, where the diadem lies walled in the hall. Beyond the Melty Pass they kept a road over a glacier that nobody has kept since, and eastern provinces sent tribute over the ice. While their garrisons held the old western march of the kingdom of the bridge, their claim to have restored it looked like the truth.

plate.subject: a great sealed stone door at the end of a dark road deep under a mountain

paragraphs.text: Four dwarf holds keep one tongue across the seas: Kunhrim in the Great Wall range, Hrakbrund under the High Mountains of the North Lands, and Brundahrim and Gromkerm in the western ranges. The names of a western hold and of a northern one are built from the same words. Each hold keeps a sealed Sea-Door at the head of an old road that once ran on under the sea.

The common speech remembers those roads as the Stone Roads, and Brunek of the Stone Roads, a dwarf engineer of the First Age, bears their name. They joined the western ranges, the Great Wall range and the High Mountains of the North beneath the floor of the Crown Sea and the Narrow Strait.

In Volgan’s war the Damned Spirits rose from deep beneath the mountains and came into the roads. The roads under the sea were broken and the sea was let in, and the holds were cut off from one another. They have had no Deep King since.
paragraphs.note: The rising of the Damned Spirits is established; the Letting-In of the Sea is adopted (K64).

paragraphs.text: Who gave the order is disputed. Kunhrim says that the Deep King ordered the Letting-In of the Sea. The western holds say that Kunhrim’s lords urged it to save their own gate, and that grudge is older than any charter. The holds believe that the sea is the seal, and that while the sea lies on what was drowned, what is in it stays. What remains below the sea, no chronicle tells.

When the western door was sealed, the fire-hold of Brundahrim carried one fire out of the drowning road in an iron fire-pot, and keeps it still as the Road-Fire. No chronicle tells where the dwarves first came from.

The holds’ own name for their realm is Gromatrak, the stone road in their tongue. It was the only realm that ever spanned three landmasses, and a dwarf could walk from the West Lands to the North Lands without seeing the sky. Its first roads were cut long before Aen, beneath the low country while it was still dry land, and they outlived its drowning because they ran in deep rock.

Its seat was Tromahrim, the Great Hall of the Deep King, deep beneath the low country’s northern hills, which are now the floor of the Sea of Monsters. Through the Western Gate, opened about 1A 300, Gromatrak sold its iron to Aenor. It sent its engineers to Dardan. When the spirits came into the roads, the Deep King let the sea in, and Tromahrim drowned with the spirits inside it.

plate.subject: a square of broken reefs and old wrecks in a grey sea under a low sky

paragraphs.text: In the Pupor Sea lies the Cursed Square, a square of reefs that wrecks ships. The islanders hold that it is cursed, and the corsairs of Benan, who hold it in name, will not sail into it whatever the prize. After the Wreck of the Square, about 2A 1507, the glass-blowers of the Lens swore to keep the passages lit.

The isles of the three arcs keep the pieces of a league of the chart-islanders, which the common speech calls the Sea-Roads. In Volgan’s war it carried the supply fleets of the Grand Alliance, under its admiral Senra. It kept the first lit passages and drew the first great charts, and it leased harbours on the coasts of the West Lands and the Cold Lands but never conquered land.

A sickness, the Grey Breath, came on the ships that served the league, and its own fleets carried it to every isle. The outer isles emptied and corsairs took their harbours; Straton fell to them in 2A 130. The league broke into chart-houses, brokers and corsair captaincies. Whether the Grey Breath still waits in the wrecks of the Square, the islanders do not agree.

Adel’s Chart Hall descends from the league’s chart-office, Raerby’s banks-court was its court for the banks, Pollos’s strong-room was its treasury, and the Lamp-House of the Lens keeps its lights. At the close of every gale season the islanders read the Drowned Names, and the oldest of them belong to no isle where anyone lives.

The league’s own name was Margorodai, the sea-road in the Tritonic tongue. It was sworn about 1A 820, when Aenor’s decline left the western sea-roads unguarded, and its height lay between 1A 1100 and 1675. It held the three arcs, the Pupor and the sea-roads from the Cold Lands ports to the Islands of the South, and at sea it was greater than Aenor ever was.

Its seat was Halgohavnai, the Holy Harbour, whose four moles on the reef shelf made a harbour where any ship under any banner paid one due. The Grey Breath came into Halgohavnai on the league’s own ships, and the harbour was left to its dead and never relit. In the gale season of 2A 904 its moles broke, and its walls became the Cursed Square. Adel’s oldest charts still show the harbour.

plate.subject: the timbers of an ancient hall and a bronze ship-prow emerging from melting ice on a frozen plain

paragraphs.text: In mild summers the ice of the Frozen Lands gives back great timber halls and bronze ship-prows. The north remembers the land they came from as the Sunfields. Long before Aen, when the ice lay far to the north, the first men of the north-west held the Fandan meadows, the interior that is now frozen, and the west coast below the Icy Mountains.

They had bronze, great timber halls and horse-herds in the Fandan meadows, and theirs was the first sea-craft of Aoaz. Then the winters lengthened over many lifetimes, and the ice came a little farther south in every age. The fields failed, the halls emptied, and the realm broke into clans.

Coldor’s fire-keepers say the land was punished. The ice giants of Nivaros say that the snow breathes in and out over the ages. The Winter Hearth, which relights every house-fire from the clan fire, is said to be the custom of the last hall, and the fire-keepers of the Frost-Hall call the hearth older than any crown.

The Neck Road over the Neridor Gap was already known to the clans when they showed it to Aenor’s surveyors about 1A 400. The snowline fair at Fentene is held on an old market-ground under the moss. The people of Mp’E believe that the Watcher in the Hall is a sleeping king of the old north.

The scholars who compare the northern tongues call the land Heulufaenn, the sun-fields. The ice clans and Coldor’s fire-keepers call it Heulfaenn, the clans of the West Lands sing of Faenn-Cheulu, and the chart-islanders name it Heulofaennos: three peoples keep three names for one lost land without knowing it. Its king’s hall was Tawrhalwe, and tawr, king, is a word all three tongues still share.

No one worked its fall. When the fields failed its people went three ways: south over the neck, where they became the Gunwyn clans of the West Lands; west by sea to the arcs, where they became the Tritonic islanders; and into the Long Dark, where the clans who stayed became the Coldic ice clans. The islanders’ words for reef, strait, cape and tide are the words of the Sunfields’ sailors.
